To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
chronic exposure of mouse islets to the cannabinoid receptor agonist ACEA or JWW015 does not compromise islet function.
chronic exposure of isolated islets to cannabinergic compounds does not affect their viability, morphology and insulin and glucagon secretion.
chronic activation of cannabinoid CB1 receptors does not compromise mouse β-cell function.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the endocannabionoid system in pancreatic islet function.
the ECS in islets and how it might contribute to the development of Type 2 diabetes.
the ECS in the islet and how it may be involved in Type 2 diabetes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
chronic activation of cannabinoid CB1 and CB2 receptors has no effect on mouse pancreatic islet function.
the chronic activation of cannabinoid receptor in vitro does not compromise mouse pancreatic islet function.
the ECS is not involved in islet dysfunction, but this conclusion may be premature and further research is needed.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ECS does not play a significant role in the pathophysiology of Type 2 diabetes.
the ECS is not a major player in islet dysfunction in Type 2 diabetics.
the ECS is not involved in the pathogenesis of T2D.
The main takeaway from our work is that

prolonged activation of the ECS in mouse islets is not deleterious, but it is possible that the effects of the ECS on β-cell function and glucagon secretion may be differentially modulated depending on the glucose concentration.
the chronic activation of cannabinoid CB1 and CB2 receptors has no effect on islet viability or insulin secretory responses.
the ECS is not implicated in islet β-cell dysfunction, at least in mice, but may play a role in the development of insulin resistance in diabetes.
